Regarding J. W. Hampton, one commentator wrote:
The general policy of the act [at issue] is fairly certain but an analysis 
of the act and even more the history of its administration shows a 
tremendous scope for manipulation. Comparative costs are difficult 
to discover, particularly in remote parts of the world; and there is 
little agreement on their evaluation. How much labor, interest on 
investment, [or] depreciation should be attributed to a unit of 
production? On every one of these items economists differ depending 
on the end in view. And what really is the premise of this legislation? 
Did “equalize” mean to enable the local producer to maintain his old 
rate of profit or merely to survive? Furthermore, administration was 
entirely dependent on presidential initiative. The President’s 
investigations were to be conducted by the Tariff Commission whose 
findings he might ignore. Mr. Chief Justice Taft labored to make 
these powers as modest and automatic as possible.
Louis L. Jaffe, Judicial Control of Administrative Action 59-60 (1965).
A.L.A. Sc h e c h t e r  Po u l t r y  Co r p. v . Un it e d  St a t e s
United States Supreme Court, 1935 
295 U.S. 495, 55 S. Ct. 837, 79 L.Ed. 1570
Mr . Ch ie f  Ju s t ic e Hu g h e s delivered the opinion of the Court.
Petitioners in No. 854 were convicted in the District Court of the 
United States for the Eastern District of New York on eighteen counts of 
an indictment charging violations of what is known as the “Live Poultry 
Code,” and on an additional count for conspiracy to commit such violations. 
* * * [T]he defendants contended * * * that the Code had been adopted 
pursuant to an unconstitutional delegation by Congress of legislative 
power * * *.
The Circuit Court of Appeals sustained the conviction on the 
conspiracy count and on sixteen counts for violation of the Code[.] * * * 
[T]his Court granted writs of certiorari * * *.
* * *
The “Live Poultry Code” was promulgated under § 3 of the National 
Industrial Recovery Act. That section * * * authorizes the President to 
approve “codes of fair competition.” Such a code may be approved for a 
trade or industry, upon application by one or more trade or industrial 
associations or groups, if the President finds (1) that such associations or 
groups “impose no inequitable restrictions on admission to membership 
therein and are truly representative,” and (2) that such codes are not
